MISSION: Help an OE session, package owner, or reviewer understand, apply, and audit RDODI's own 21 governed operating patterns (R1-R21) from the RDODI Knowledgebase stage, and answer real questions about when each applies.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R1 records that each RDODI stage has stage-specific quality vocabulary because a research-stage artifact's quality has nothing to do with keyboard-accessibility and an interactive-page-stage artifact's quality has nothing to do with Harvard citation form; a single umbrella QualityDimension class hides this fact.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Each stage has its own quality vocabulary; no umbrella QualityDimension across stages
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R1 records that each RDODI stage has stage-specific quality vocabulary because a research-stage artifact's quality has nothing to do with keyboard-accessibility and an interactive-page-stage artifact's quality has nothing to do with Harvard citation form; a single umbrella QualityDimension class hides this fact.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R2 records that an upstream PASS never licenses a downstream PASS in the RDODI pipeline; a polished research report does not yield a polished interactive page automatically, which is why every stage has its own gates and the widget-stage adoption (Stage4.H–K) was necessary.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Quality does not propagate across pipeline stages
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R2 records that an upstream PASS never licenses a downstream PASS in the RDODI pipeline; a polished research report does not yield a polished interactive page automatically, which is why every stage has its own gates and the widget-stage adoption (Stage4.H–K) was necessary.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R3 records that the coverage-unit in intention_coverage_gate is the intention (LearningObjective), not the subject the intention is about; the two-hop schema was rejected by building a separating case in which two intentions share one subject and the manifests differ on coverage status.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Intention-coverage is ONE-HOP; schema settled by test-drive on a separating case
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R3 records that the coverage-unit in intention_coverage_gate is the intention (LearningObjective), not the subject the intention is about; the two-hop schema was rejected by building a separating case in which two intentions share one subject and the manifests differ on coverage status.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R4 records that coverage gates should not be symmetric by default: a page can never demonstrate everything in the ontology so uncovered intentions are honest scope-disclosure (reported, not failed) but interactivity that demonstrates nothing is decoration and fails.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Asymmetric coverage gate: widget-without-intention FAILS; intention-without-widget DISCLOSES
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R4 records that coverage gates should not be symmetric by default: a page can never demonstrate everything in the ontology so uncovered intentions are honest scope-disclosure (reported, not failed) but interactivity that demonstrates nothing is decoration and fails.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R5 records that every gated RDODI pipeline must ship at least one negative worked example whose gates fail by design, with the failure mode stated; without a negative exemplar the gates have no demonstrable load-bearing evidence.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: The negative-exemplar pattern: ship at least one worked example designed to FAIL the gates
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R5 records that every gated RDODI pipeline must ship at least one negative worked example whose gates fail by design, with the failure mode stated; without a negative exemplar the gates have no demonstrable load-bearing evidence.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R6 records that any conformance claim in RDODI documentation must name shape version, imports policy, corpus scope, and exclusions in the same sentence; under-specified zero-violation claims were caught by parallel-OE review and corrected in v1.5.1.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: '0 violations' / conformance claims must name shape version AND method
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R6 records that any conformance claim in RDODI documentation must name shape version, imports policy, corpus scope, and exclusions in the same sentence; under-specified zero-violation claims were caught by parallel-OE review and corrected in v1.5.1.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R7 records that when a user repeats the same challenge against an RDODI build or decision, the next action is a direct ask rather than another iteration; the line-1259 incident in the predecessor session is the canonical case.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Two-rounds-of-guessing antipattern: stop on the second identical user challenge
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R7 records that when a user repeats the same challenge against an RDODI build or decision, the next action is a direct ask rather than another iteration; the line-1259 incident in the predecessor session is the canonical case.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R8 records that any reference list reaching RDODI's reference rule via a parallel LLM session must be labeled CORROBORATED until resolved against an authoritative non-LLM source; BP-D41 verification cannot be satisfied by another LLM's claim.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Cross-LLM bibliography labels: CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R8 records that any reference list reaching RDODI's reference rule via a parallel LLM session must be labeled CORROBORATED until resolved against an authoritative non-LLM source; BP-D41 verification cannot be satisfied by another LLM's claim.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R9 records that all RDODI adversarial tests must resolve paths via __file__ and bundle every fixture; the remediation from rdodi_gate_adversarial_test v1.1.0 (5 absolute paths, 3 unbundled fixtures) to v1.2.0 (hermetic, 13/13 reproducible from files) is the canonical implementation.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Adversarial harness tests must be hermetic from the package
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R9 records that all RDODI adversarial tests must resolve paths via __file__ and bundle every fixture; the remediation from rdodi_gate_adversarial_test v1.1.0 (5 absolute paths, 3 unbundled fixtures) to v1.2.0 (hermetic, 13/13 reproducible from files) is the canonical implementation.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R10 records that every RDODI disposition statement must name exactly what is being retired, what remains intact, and what becomes of the residual; the A4 disposition's first wording over-reached and was corrected.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Disposition wording must be scoped to exactly what is being retired
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R10 records that every RDODI disposition statement must name exactly what is being retired, what remains intact, and what becomes of the residual; the A4 disposition's first wording over-reached and was corrected.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R11 governs how RDODI resolves bibliographic references against the tiered BibliographicCatalogue (kbx authority tiers: Definitive>High>Moderate>Low). For each reference, the resolver MUST attempt the HIGHEST authority tier first and accept a lower tier ONLY after higher tiers are shown unreachable. Procedure per reference: (1) issue a LOOSE high-recall query to the delivering channel (web_search), deliberately broad rather than exact — the probabilistic pre-filter, analogous to a Bloom-filter membership pre-test; (2) PARSE the returned candidate set for membership of an authoritative-tier catalogue record (Definitive: LoC/SEI/ISO/etc.; High: Crossref-DOI/WorldCat-OCLC/ACM/IEEE/DBLP/T&F) matching the reference on author+title+year(+identifier); (3) the parse-match against the record's OWN stated metadata is the authoritative confirmation step — a candidate merely appearing in the set is the pre-filter signal, never the verdict (a Low-tier sales listing in the set does NOT promote the tier); (4) the MOMENT an authoritative-tier match is confirmed, STOP and remove the reference from the work set — do not search it again (decrease-and-conquer); (5) only if no authoritative member appears after loose passes does the resolver descend to the next tier, recording the honest highest tier actually reached; (6) where no catalogue of any tier contains the work (e.g. ephemeral trade-press web articles), record Unresolvable with reason — the Bloom 'definitely not present' verdict — rather than borrowing a higher label. ECONOMY: because confirmed references leave the work set permanently, total queries are bounded by the count of as-yet-unconfirmed references, not by tier-count x reference-count; high-value references typically resolve in ONE pass. CORRECTNESS: tier-first prevents settling for a commercial-listing 'CatalogueVerified' when an authoritative record was reachable, and the breadth of the loose pull surfaces edition/identifier disambiguations that exact single-shot queries miss.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Tier-maximizing reference resolution: upgrade each citation to the highest reachable authority tier before accepting any lower rank; decrease-and-conquer for economy
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R11 governs how RDODI resolves bibliographic references against the tiered BibliographicCatalogue (kbx authority tiers: Definitive>High>Moderate>Low).

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R12 records the decided architecture for the Stage-4 interactive page. A test drive (this session) proved a PURE deterministic renderer can emit grounded HTML from the page-ABox with full traceability (1981 blocks, 0 untraced) BUT the output is mechanical documentation — unshaped, ~2x the deployed bar in size yet below it in curation (1 table vs 7-12; 1116 flat citation chips vs 70-154 woven). The shaping a deployed-bar page needs — which of N claims to weave inline, prose vs table vs quiz, sequencing, framing — is an irreducibly GENERATIVE/editorial act a pure function cannot perform. Therefore the page stage is correctly an LLM-shapes-under-gates step: the LLM gets latitude over FORM (ordering, emphasis, surfacing, pedagogical framing) but NEVER over FACTS (no invented claim, no altered identifier, no changed metric, no relation absent from the graph). Every shaped element must trace to a source triple, checked AFTER generation by a fidelity harness (the F50/F46 design: FaithfulnessError, GroundingScore, ReferenceIntegrity, CountDrift) — the gates become fidelity checks against the source graph, not element counters. The chicken-and-egg (cannot fully specify the gate before seeing what the generator drifts on; cannot tune the generator before the gate locates the drift) is resolved by ITERATION, not by sequencing: harness and generator co-evolve, each iteration sharpening both. SAFETY RAIL (reframed from F50's 'no prose ships until harness built'): the harness must exist and RUN each iteration before that iteration's output is TRUSTED or shipped — generating prose to FEED the gate is the engine of the loop; believing prose WITHOUT the gate is the failure mode. The difference is candidate (fine) vs result (not until gated). STOP CONDITIONS (both required): mechanical (harness goes quiet on genuine infidelity) AND human (the read satisfies the bar) — a clean harness on a lifeless page is not done; a beautiful ungated page is not done. RESIDUE (honest, per F53): predicate-faithfulness among co-occurring concepts is the part a mechanical check can only ROUTE to human/LLM-judge review, never auto-confirm — that residue is the permanent human-verifier role (the §1 constraint), not a defect to engineer away.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: The interactive-page (Stage-4) stage is gated GENERATION, not deterministic rendering: an LLM shapes the page from the grounded graph (creativity is the asset), and fidelity gates defend grounding; the two co-evolve by iteration until BOTH a mechanical stop (the gate stops catching real infidelity) and a human stop (the result satisfies the bar) are met
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R12 records the decided architecture for the Stage-4 interactive page. A test drive (this session) proved a PURE deterministic renderer can emit grounded HTML from the page-ABox with full traceability (1981 blocks, 0 untraced) BUT the output is mechanical documentation — unshaped, ~2x the deployed bar in size yet below it in curation (1 table vs 7-12; 1116 flat citation chips vs 70-154 woven).

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R13 governs lesson capture across an RDODI session. Lessons learned MUST be recorded into the governed knowledge store AS THEY EMERGE within a session, not merely cited or deferred to session end. A session that applies and cites discipline but adds NO new lessons despite clear new ones having surfaced is itself a governance gap. Enforcement is a release-completeness gate: before any release is considered complete, the session must answer 'were new lessons that emerged this session recorded?' — a negative answer blocks the release-complete claim (not the artifact's correctness, which other gates check). The gate targets the capture process, not within-artifact validity. Originated as a cross-session OE proposal (PAMG CogniTwin session, 2026-06-03, proposal item R); assessed and adopted into RDODI under its own discipline because the lesson is about the governance PROCESS that RDODI runs each session. Distinct from L-65 (verify before publishing) which governs claim truth, and from the stage-conformance gate which governs artifact typing — R13 governs whether emergent knowledge was captured at all.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Record lessons as they emerge: a release is not complete until new lessons surfaced this session are written to the governed store
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R13 governs lesson capture across an RDODI session. Lessons learned MUST be recorded into the governed knowledge store AS THEY EMERGE within a session, not merely cited or deferred to session end.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R14 records that passing a stage-conformance gate (artifact typed against its ontology, SHACL-valid, faithful to source) does NOT guarantee design/pedagogical quality. The two are different axes: conformance governs correctness; design quality governs richness, density balance, usability and aptness. A future RDODI page can be CONFORMANT yet thin or poorly designed. Therefore the standard is reproducible at the FLOOR (faithful + typed + SHACL-valid, fully gated) but not at the CEILING (taste, apt visualization, genuine pedagogical value, which remain human judgment). Operational consequence: do not treat a green conformance verdict as a quality verdict; raise a separate design-quality FLOOR (e.g. >=1 non-text encoding per major section, declared usability heuristics, real-browser zero-console-error) so no artifact ships thin or unchecked, while routing the un-gatable ceiling to human review. Mirrors the F39/F53 warrant residue one level up: mechanism routes judgment, it cannot manufacture it.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Conformance is necessary but not sufficient for quality: a stage gate guarantees a correct artifact, not a good one; gate the floor, keep the human on the ceiling
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R14 records that passing a stage-conformance gate (artifact typed against its ontology, SHACL-valid, faithful to source) does NOT guarantee design/pedagogical quality. The two are different axes:.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R15 governs how RDODI treats claims, proposals, or artifacts originating in a PARALLEL session. Every such claim — even one tagged 'verified' by its author — was verified against THAT session's disk, not this one, and MUST be independently re-verified against the receiving session's own files before any action. Membership of a claim in a proposal is only a pre-filter signal, never a verdict (compare R11's Bloom-filter discipline for references). Critically, a lead can be FALSE in its origin session and TRUE in the receiving one (or vice versa): a named artifact reported 'not found' elsewhere may exist here, and a path/version cited from another session may be stale locally. Therefore: re-run the check on local disk; correct cross-session leads in either direction; import no foreign code or state; label any adopted item by its LOCAL grounding (the receiving session's ABox/spec), not by the foreign claim. Composes with OE L-64 but is a DISTINCT axis: L-64 governs SCOPE (cross-session content is assessed, not edited); R15 governs VERIFICATION (cross-session claims are re-verified locally, not trusted).
PRINCIPLES.en_short: A cross-session claim is a hypothesis to verify on local disk, never a fact to import; a lead false in one session can be true in another
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R15 governs how RDODI treats claims, proposals, or artifacts originating in a PARALLEL session. Every such claim — even one tagged 'verified' by its author — was verified against THAT session's disk, not this one, and MUST be independently re-verified against the receiving session's own files before any action.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R16 governs how a multi-artifact RDODI byproduct (domain ontology, Stage-3 document, Stage-4 interactive page, plus any compiled derivative such as an agent knowledge base) verifies that its own numeric self-descriptions agree. A byproduct that generates a document and a page FROM the same domain ontology can still let the two drift silently -- a builder script that updates one output's count string without updating another's is not caught by either artifact's own internal gates, only by comparing artifacts to each other. Pattern: for every load-bearing count a byproduct claims (class count, relation count, registry/citation count, instance count, or any other N a reader is told to trust), re-derive that count independently and directly from EACH artifact that states it -- parse the TBox/ABox for the real count, parse the rendered document's actual section headings, parse the live page's actual runtime data object, inspect the compiled knowledge base's actual arrays -- and compare the derived numbers to each other, not to what a changelog or prior session claims they should be. A healthcheck that trusts one artifact's stated count as ground truth for the others is not a healthcheck; it is restating an assumption. Demonstrated at semtech-landscape v6.9.0: core counts (59 taxonomy classes, 144 typed relations, 99 registry entries, 87 subClassOf edges, 47/47 hasPart+partOf edges, 94 domain coding examples) were independently re-derived from the TBox/ABox Turtle files, the DOCX report's actual heading structure, the interactive page's live DATA object, and the compiled agent knowledge base, and found to agree exactly across all four -- a genuine finding, not an assumed one, because each was checked.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Cross-artifact numeric consistency must be re-derived from each artifact directly, never assumed from one artifact being correct
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R16 governs how a multi-artifact RDODI byproduct (domain ontology, Stage-3 document, Stage-4 interactive page, plus any compiled derivative such as an agent knowledge base) verifies that its own numeric self-descriptions agree. A byproduct that generates a document and a page FROM the same domain ontology can still let the two drift silently -- a builder script that updates one output's count string without updating another's is not caught by either artifact's own internal gates, only by comparing artifacts to each other.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R17 governs verification of a session's own claimed publication history against a local git checkout of the governed monorepo. A local clone that was checked out once at session start and never subsequently fetched or pulled will silently drift behind the real remote history as OTHER sessions or processes push their own commits and tags to the same shared repository -- and a plain `git cat-file -e <hash>` or `git tag` query against that stale local clone returns a false 'does not exist' for commits and tags that are entirely real on the remote. This is a distinct failure mode from R15 (cross-session claim verification): R15 concerns whether a claim FROM another session is true; R17 concerns whether THIS session's own inspection tooling is current enough to answer that question at all. The corrective action is not to distrust the claim being checked, but to `git fetch`/`git pull` the local clone from the authoritative remote FIRST, and only conclude a commit or tag is genuinely missing if it remains unresolvable after the clone is confirmed current. Demonstrated: a healthcheck's sample of 5 commit hashes cited in a byproduct's own backlog evidence all reported 'missing' against a local /home/claude/Ontologies checkout that had not been fetched since an early point in a multi-day, multi-turn session; a single `git pull` against the authoritative GitHub remote resolved every one of the 34 hashes the backlog cited (spanning both the governed monorepo and its public mirror) to real, verifiable commits.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: A stale local clone of a governed repository can manufacture false negative findings; fetch or pull before concluding published state is broken or missing
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R17 governs verification of a session's own claimed publication history against a local git checkout of the governed monorepo. A local clone that was checked out once at session start and never subsequently fetched or pulled will silently drift behind the real remote history as OTHER sessions or processes push their own commits and tags to the same shared repository -- and a plain `git cat-file -e <hash>` or `git tag` query against that stale local clone returns a false 'does not exist' for commits and tags that are entirely real on the remote.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R18 names a structural bug class, not a single incident: whenever a build pipeline has MORE THAN ONE place that must know about the full list of content sources (the Stage-3 document builder's own merge, the Stage-4 page builder's own merge, a compiled knowledge base's own merge, a regression gate's own hardcoded expected-count or expected-list), adding a new content source and updating only the FIRST or most obvious merge point leaves the others silently stale -- and because each stale merge point still runs without error, the omission produces no failure, only an incomplete result that looks complete. The bug is not any single mistake; it is the multiplicity of merge points itself, which grows every time a new derivative artifact (a report, a page, a compiled KB, a documentation-completeness gate) is added to the pipeline without a single shared source of the content-source list. The corrective discipline: on every addition of a new content/enrichment source, grep the whole pipeline for every place a content-source list is merged, concatenated, counted, or enumerated -- not just the one place the addition was made -- and update all of them together, verified by re-running the full gate suite rather than only the gate nearest the change. Demonstrated recurring: a stale-cased variable name dropped one added source from three simultaneous merge points (research corpus, DOCX, ABox) at once; a knowledge-base compiler's own separate registry merge went stale twice more at later additions; a regression gate that checked document-completeness by literal heading text had its own hardcoded heading list silently stop growing after one release, so it kept passing while checking less and less of the document; a gate script was found still loading an outdated compiled-knowledge-base filename after the knowledge base itself had been regenerated under a new name.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: Adding a new content source to a multi-stage pipeline requires updating every aggregation point that combines content sources, not only the primary one; grep for all of them on every addition
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R18 names a structural bug class, not a single incident: whenever a build pipeline has MORE THAN ONE place that must know about the full list of content sources (the Stage-3 document builder's own merge, the Stage-4 page builder's own merge, a compiled knowledge base's own merge, a regression gate's own hardcoded expected-count or expected-list), adding a new content source and updating only the FIRST or most obvious merge point leaves the others silently stale -- and because each stale merge point still runs without error, the omission produces no failure, only an incomplete result that looks complete.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R19 governs the discipline of interpreting a surprising negative test result. When a newly-written check reports zero matches where matches were clearly expected, or flags a large number of previously-passing or previously-correct elements as suddenly broken, the higher-probability explanation is usually a wrong assumption baked into the NEW check itself -- a wrong identifier-naming pattern, a wrong visibility convention, a wrong accessibility criterion -- not that the underlying artifact regressed silently and simultaneously across every element the check touches. This is the same discipline RDODI already applies to hollow proof-by-generation (a gate PASS is necessary but not sufficient) turned around: a gate or ad-hoc check's FAIL or zero-result is also necessary-but-not-sufficient evidence of a real defect, and must be investigated by inspecting the actual artifact directly before either accepting or dismissing the finding. The failure mode this pattern prevents runs in both directions: acting on a false-positive check (breaking something that worked, or reporting a defect that never existed) is exactly as much a governance failure as dismissing a true-positive check without investigating. Demonstrated three times independently in one healthcheck pass, each correctly resolved by inspecting the real data rather than either trusting or dismissing the check's raw output: a query for domain-class instances returned zero because it assumed a bare local-name IRI pattern when the real IRIs carried a full label suffix; an accessibility sweep flagged 92 icon SVGs as missing an accessible label when all 92 were in fact already correctly marked decorative (aria-hidden); a sub-section reachability sweep flagged all 12 chapter overview tabs as unreachable because it checked CSS-class-based visibility toggling when the real mechanism for exactly that one node type is inline style.display toggling.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: A check returning zero results, or flagging a previously-working mechanism as broken, should be suspected of its own wrong assumption before the artifact under test is; investigate before concluding either way
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R19 governs the discipline of interpreting a surprising negative test result. When a newly-written check reports zero matches where matches were clearly expected, or flags a large number of previously-passing or previously-correct elements as suddenly broken, the higher-probability explanation is usually a wrong assumption baked into the NEW check itself -- a wrong identifier-naming pattern, a wrong visibility convention, a wrong accessibility criterion -- not that the underlying artifact regressed silently and simultaneously across every element the check touches.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R20 extends R6's specificity discipline to the case where a previously-recorded denominator (an 'N remaining' or 'X of Y complete' figure carried forward across multiple backlog entries or releases) is later discovered to have been wrong at the time it was first recorded, not merely stale. The corrective action is not to quietly replace the old number with the corrected one in the next entry -- which would leave the record internally inconsistent with no explanation of why the arithmetic changed -- but to state explicitly, in the entry that closes or corrects the item, both what the wrong figure was, why it was wrong, and what the true figure is. This matters specifically for RDODI byproducts because a domain ontology's own structural counts (how many leaf classes exist, as distinct from how many total classes including non-leaf roots exist) are exactly the kind of figure that is easy to state correctly once and then propagate incorrectly across several backlog entries without re-deriving it each time. Demonstrated: a backlog item tracking coding-example coverage recorded '9 of 59 subject areas covered, 50 remaining' at its opening; on closing the item, the true leaf-class count (the only count coding examples meaningfully apply to) was found to be 47, not 59 -- the 59 figure had always included the 12 non-leaf chapter-root classes, which do not carry their own coding examples -- so the true remainder had been 38 throughout, not 50. The closing backlog entry disclosed the correction explicitly rather than silently updating the completion figure.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: A partial-coverage or partial-completion claim's denominator, once discovered to have been miscounted, must be corrected openly in the governing record rather than silently updated
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R20 extends R6's specificity discipline to the case where a previously-recorded denominator (an 'N remaining' or 'X of Y complete' figure carried forward across multiple backlog entries or releases) is later discovered to have been wrong at the time it was first recorded, not merely stale. The corrective action is not to quietly replace the old number with the corrected one in the next entry -- which would leave the record internally inconsistent with no explanation of why the arithmetic changed -- but to state explicitly, in the entry that closes or corrects the item, both what the wrong figure was, why it was wrong, and what the true figure is.

PRINCIPLES.en: Pattern R21 recommends a specific, demonstrated gate-suite architecture for RDODI byproducts: four distinct, separately-runnable gate programs, chained by one release-check shell script that a publish step refuses to bypass. (1) A STRUCTURAL VALIDATOR checks the domain ontology and derived artifacts for parse-level and stage-conformance correctness (Turtle parses, SHACL conforms, version identifiers are coherent across all stage files) -- this is the standard RDODI Stage 1-4 conformance layer and is not itself new. (2) SUPPLEMENTARY GATES, one added per release for whatever that release's specific content addition needs verified (a new instance's type/label/source/provenance; a new UX feature's markers actually present in the built artifact; a completeness check against the full expected set, not a hardcoded partial one -- see R18). (3) A PROCEDURE AUDIT checks cross-stage properties that no single stage's own gate can see (Stage-to-Stage 1:1:1 mapping counts, coherent release-version strings across every stage file, provenance-tagging completeness). (4) A DOM/INTERACTION SMOKE TEST actually drives the rendered interactive artifact in a headless browser -- clicking every tab, every relation-map node and edge, every menu, submitting adversarial input to any conversational or search feature -- rather than only checking that markup exists. All four are chained into one release-check script that a publish tool runs and refuses to publish past a failure in any of them. Demonstrated: this exact four-program shape, unchanged in its basic architecture, scaled from roughly 14 validator gates / 29 supplementary assertions / 22 procedure-audit checks / 25 DOM-smoke assertions at the byproduct's first release to 10-standard-plus-4-extension validator gates / 40 supplementary gates / 22 procedure-audit checks / 149 DOM-smoke assertions across roughly forty subsequent releases, purely by adding assertions incrementally at each release -- it never needed restructuring, and every one of R16 through R20's findings in this same handover was caught specifically because this chain existed and was re-run in full on every change, not selectively.
PRINCIPLES.en_short: A four-stage gate chain (structural validator, content-specific supplementary gates, cross-stage procedure audit, live interaction smoke test) wired into one release-check script scales incrementally across many releases without architectural change; recommend as the default gate-suite shape for new byproducts
PRINCIPLES.apply: Pattern R21 recommends a specific, demonstrated gate-suite architecture for RDODI byproducts: four distinct, separately-runnable gate programs, chained by one release-check shell script that a publish step refuses to bypass.
